source.notes: Top-down studio photograph of a MOS MPS6502B in a 40-pin plastic DIP, date code 3980 (week 39 of 1980), by Commons user ZyMOS (own work), CC BY-SA 4.0 per the Commons API extmetadata. Chosen for sharpness and a clean top-down view; the exhibited part is a 1980 plastic-package example of the 1975 design. The chip is shown enlarged: the photograph of a 5 cm part hangs at about a metre wide. An earlier example, a white-ceramic MCS6502 from week 45 of 1975, is recorded as an alternate representation.

alternates.notes: A MOS Technology MCS6502 in a white ceramic 40-pin package with a gold lid, date code 4575 (week 45 of 1975), only a few months after the 6502 was introduced; by Commons user Christian Bassow, CC BY-SA 4.0. The most historic example found on Commons, but only 640 px wide, so it is the alternate rather than the shown image.

object.medium: 8-bit NMOS microprocessor in a 40-pin dual in-line package

creator.name: Chuck Peddle and the MOS Technology design team

object.description: The 6502 is the 8-bit microprocessor that made the personal computer affordable. Chuck Peddle and a small team at MOS Technology, several of them fresh from Motorola's 6800, designed it to sell for $25 when the 6800 and Intel's 8080 cost around $179, and introduced it at the Wescon show in San Francisco in September 1975. It ran the Apple I and Apple II, the Commodore PET and VIC-20, the BBC Micro and, as variants, the Commodore 64, the Atari 2600 and the Nintendo Entertainment System. The Apple IIc beside it runs the 65C02, a low-power CMOS version of this chip.
facts: Launched at $25 in September 1975; MOS sold them from a jar at the Wescon show, and the price forced Motorola and Intel to cut theirs.
About 3,500 transistors on a die a few millimetres across, drawn by hand; the design clocked at 1 MHz.
Steve Wozniak chose it for the Apple I because it was the only processor he could afford.
